parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: Radioactive decay is both random and spontaneous.
parts.text: State what is meant by random.

markscheme_points.text: cannot predict when a particular nucleus will decay or cannot predict which nucleus will decay next

hints: Hint 1: Think about the difference between what you can say about a huge sample with activity and half-life, and what you can say about one single identified nucleus in that sample.
parts.proper_answer: Random means it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay, or which nucleus will decay next.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What random really means**
Think of sitting with thousands of identical unstable nuclei. You know as a group they decay with a steady average rate, but random means each individual nucleus keeps its secret. There is no clock or warning.

Step 2: **Examiner-perfect wording**
So you say it clearly: you cannot predict when a particular nucleus will decay. Every nucleus has the same probability of decaying in the next second, but which one goes next is purely chance.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: State what is meant by spontaneous.

markscheme_points.text: (decay is) not affected by external (environmental) factors

hints: Hint 1: Ask yourself whether heating, cooling, squeezing, or putting the source in a chemical compound or magnetic field can force it to decay faster or stop it decaying.
parts.proper_answer: Spontaneous means decay is not affected by external factors such as temperature, pressure or chemical environment.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What spontaneous really means**
Spontaneous does not mean sudden. It means self-starting with no trigger needed and no way to control it from outside. The instability is inside the nucleus itself.

Step 2: **Lock in the definition**
Changing temperature, pressure, chemical state or surroundings has no effect on the decay probability. Once a nucleus is unstable, it will decay on its own without any external influence.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: State one piece of evidence for the random nature of decay.
hints: Hint 1: Imagine you use a GM tube to count for 10 s, reset, and repeat many times with the same source in the same position - would you expect exactly the same count every time if decay were regular?
parts.proper_answer: Repeated measurements of count rate over equal time intervals show random fluctuations about a mean value.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Linking idea to experiment**
If decay were regular like a clock, a detector placed near a long half-life source would give almost exactly the same number of counts in every equal time interval.

Step 2: **What you actually see**
In practice the counts jump up and down unpredictably around an average, even after allowing for background. Those fluctuations in measured count rate are direct evidence that emission happens at random times.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Describe the differences between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.

markscheme_points.text: large nuclei undergo fission whereas small nuclei undergo fusion; fission involves one nucleus splitting into two (or more) (smaller) nuclei; fusion involves two nuclei joining together to form one (larger) nucleus; fission is (usually) initiated by neutron bombardment; fusion is (usually) initiated by (very) high temperatures

hints: Hint 1: Start by picturing the direction of each process - does the nucleon number go from one to many, or from many to one?
Hint 2: Now think about where on the chart of nuclei each process is useful - which process needs a very heavy starting nucleus and which needs very light starting nuclei?
Hint 3: Finally consider how each process is started in practice - what particle is fired in, and what extreme condition is needed to overcome repulsion?
parts.proper_answer: Fission is the splitting of a large heavy nucleus into two or more smaller nuclei, usually initiated by neutron bombardment. Fusion is the joining of two small light nuclei to form a single larger nucleus, usually requiring very high temperatures.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Opposite directions**
Picture fission as breaking apart: one heavy nucleus such as uranium splits into two medium-sized daughter nuclei plus neutrons. Picture fusion as building up: two light nuclei such as hydrogen isotopes join to make one heavier nucleus such as helium.

Step 2: **Large versus small starters**
Fission happens to large nuclei with high nucleon number. Fusion happens to small nuclei with low nucleon number. That is a key difference to state.

Step 3: **How they are triggered**
Fission is usually initiated by hitting the heavy nucleus with a neutron, which makes it unstable and split. Fusion needs the two positively charged nuclei to get extremely close despite electrostatic repulsion, so very high temperatures and kinetic energies are needed, as in stars.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Explain, with reference to the variation of binding energy per nucleon with nucleon number, why the processes of nuclear fission and nuclear fusion both result in a release of energy.

markscheme_points.text: binding energy per nucleon is greatest for intermediate nucleon numbers (may be shown on sketch graph with axes labelled 'binding energy per nucleon' and 'nucleon number')
both fusion and fission involve an increase in binding energy (per nucleon)

hints: Hint 1: Recall the shape of the binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number curve - where is the peak and what happens on either side for very light and very heavy nuclei?
Hint 2: Think about what an increase in binding energy per nucleon means for the total binding energy and therefore for the mass of the products compared to the reactants.
parts.proper_answer: Binding energy per nucleon is low for very light and very heavy nuclei and greatest for intermediate nucleon numbers around $A \approx 50-60$. In both fission of a heavy nucleus and fusion of light nuclei the products move toward the peak, so binding energy per nucleon increases and the excess energy is released.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember the curve**
Plot binding energy per nucleon $E_b/A$ on the y-axis against nucleon number $A$ on the x-axis. It rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks at about $8.8\text{ MeV}$ for iron region $A \approx 50$ to $60$, then falls slowly for heavy nuclei like uranium at about $7.6\text{ MeV}$.

Step 2: **Both move uphill**
In fusion, two low-$A$ nuclei with low $E_b/A$ combine to a nucleus nearer the peak with higher $E_b/A$. In fission, one high-$A$ nucleus with low $E_b/A$ splits into two medium-$A$ nuclei nearer the peak with higher $E_b/A$.

Step 3: **Why energy comes out**
Higher binding energy means the nucleons are more tightly bound, so total binding energy increases. From $$\Delta E = \Delta m c^2$$ this increase comes from a decrease in mass. The lost mass appears as kinetic energy of products and gamma photons, so energy is released in both processes.
